insurgent|subversive.distinction: An insurgent fights the state openly, while a subversive undermines it quietly from inside. One carries a weapon, the other carries a card.

interdict|proscribe.distinction: Interdict and proscribe both mean to forbid by authority, though proscribe usually bans a thing or practice outright and interdict often blocks a route or supply.

inveigle|wheedle.distinction: Inveigle carries a hint of trickery as well as flattery, while wheedle is coaxing by soft words alone. A child wheedles; a con artist inveigles.

inviolable|inviolate.distinction: Inviolable means it must never be broken, while inviolate means it has not in fact been broken. One is a rule, the other is a state.

inviolable|sacrosanct.distinction: Inviolable states that a thing must not be breached, while sacrosanct says it is treated as sacred, often with a hint that the reverence is excessive.

inviolable|unassailable.distinction: Inviolable means it must not be violated as a principle, while unassailable means no attack on it could succeed. One is moral, the other practical.

irksome|tedious.distinction: Irksome irritates, while tedious bores. A form that must be filled in monthly is irksome; a four-hour lecture is tedious.

irony|satire.distinction: Irony is the gap between what is said or expected and what is true, while satire is a whole work using humour to attack folly. Satire uses irony as a tool.

irreverent|pert.distinction: Irreverent mocks what others hold sacred, while pert is small lively cheek in ordinary company. Irreverent offends belief; pert only offends rank.

itinerant|peripatetic.distinction: Itinerant usually implies moving for work and often poverty, while peripatetic is neutral or academic. An itinerant labourer, a peripatetic music teacher.

jejune|puerile.distinction: Jejune means thin and unsatisfying in substance, while puerile means childish in a way that irritates. A jejune argument is empty; a puerile joke is immature.

jocund|jovial.distinction: Jocund is light-hearted merriment, mostly literary, while jovial is hearty sociable good humour. Jovial suits a host filling glasses; jocund suits a poem.

kindle|provoke.distinction: Kindle starts something small and growing, usually a feeling, while provoke forces a reaction, usually an angry one. Kindle interest, provoke a quarrel.

kowtow|toady.distinction: To kowtow is the act of abject deference, while a toady is the person who habitually flatters. One names the bow, the other names the courtier.

labor|toil.distinction: Labor is the general word for hard work and can also mean to belabour a point, while toil always means grinding exhausting effort.

laconic|terse.distinction: Laconic describes a person who habitually uses few words, while terse describes a particular reply that is short and often curt.

lampoon|parody.distinction: A lampoon attacks a person with ridicule, while a parody imitates a style for comic effect. A parody can be affectionate; a lampoon is not.

languish|pine.distinction: Languish is to weaken through neglect, while pine is to waste away from longing for something. A bill languishes in committee; a dog pines for its owner.

largesse|magnanimity.distinction: Largesse is open-handed giving of money, while magnanimity is refusing to press an advantage. One empties a purse, the other spares an enemy.

largess|magnanimity.distinction: Largess is generosity with money and gifts, while magnanimity is generosity of spirit toward rivals. A patron shows largess; a victor shows magnanimity.

lavish|munificent.distinction: Lavish can describe abundance of any kind and may imply excess, while munificent is only ever praise for a giver's generosity.

lavish|unsparing.distinction: Lavish is giving abundantly, while unsparing can also mean withholding no criticism. Unsparing praise is generous; unsparing judgement is harsh.

lavish|unstinting.distinction: Lavish suggests abundance that may tip into excess, while unstinting simply means nothing was held back. Unstinting support is praise; lavish spending may not be.

leery|wary.distinction: Leery and wary both mean cautious about a risk, though leery is more colloquial and carries a stronger note of distrust of the other party.

level|raze.distinction: Level can also mean to aim an accusation, while raze only ever means to destroy a building to the ground. Charges are levelled, not razed.

limpid|lucid.distinction: Limpid is clarity you can see through, as in water or a voice, while lucid is clarity you can follow, as in prose or an argument.

limpid|pellucid.distinction: Limpid and pellucid both mean perfectly clear and are interchangeable, though pellucid is the rarer and is used more often of prose than of water.

limpid|perspicuous.distinction: Limpid describes clear water or clear style, while perspicuous is only ever about expression that is easy to follow.

lissome|sinuous.distinction: Lissome describes a slim supple body, while sinuous describes a winding curving line. A dancer is lissome; a river is sinuous.

lissome|supple.distinction: Lissome combines slenderness with suppleness and suits people, while supple is about flexibility alone and suits leather and joints as readily.

lucid|pellucid.distinction: Lucid means easy to follow, while pellucid means perfectly transparent and is the more emphatic. Pellucid prose is not merely lucid but crystalline.

lucid|perspicuous.distinction: Lucid can also describe a mind that is clear-headed, while perspicuous only describes expression. A patient has lucid intervals, not perspicuous ones.

luxuriant|profuse.distinction: Luxuriant is about thick healthy growth, while profuse is about quantity poured out. Luxuriant hair grows; profuse apologies are made.

magisterial|peremptory.distinction: Magisterial commands respect by mastery, while peremptory commands obedience and allows no reply. One earns authority, the other asserts it.

malevolent|malign.distinction: Malevolent describes the wish to do harm, while malign as a verb means to speak evil of someone. One is an attitude, the other an act.

malign|traduce.distinction: Malign and traduce both mean to speak evil of someone, though traduce insists the account is false while malign leaves that open.

malleable|pliant.distinction: Malleable comes from metal under a hammer and suits minds being shaped, while pliant comes from bending and suits people who yield to pressure.

manifest|palpable.distinction: Manifest means plain to see, while palpable means so strong it feels almost physical. Manifest unfairness is visible; palpable tension is felt.

manifest|patent.distinction: Manifest and patent both mean obvious on the face of it and are interchangeable, though patent is the word law prefers for a plain falsehood or absurdity.

mar|vitiate.distinction: Mar spoils the appearance or perfection of a thing, while vitiate destroys its validity or effect. A scratch mars a table; a lie vitiates a contract.

maudlin|mawkish.distinction: Maudlin is tearful sentimentality, often from drink, while mawkish is sentimentality so thick it sickens the reader. One weeps, the other cloys.

maunder|wander.distinction: Maunder is mainly about rambling in speech, while wander is mainly about moving without a course. A speaker maunders; a walker wanders.

meander|wander.distinction: Meander stresses the winding curving path taken, while wander stresses the absence of any destination. A river meanders; a mind wanders.

meretricious|specious.distinction: Meretricious is showily attractive and cheap underneath, while specious is plausible in argument and false underneath. One fools the eye, the other the reason.

meretricious|tawdry.distinction: Meretricious implies a deliberate false attractiveness, while tawdry is simply cheap and gaudy. Tawdry decoration is not trying to deceive anyone.

metamorphose|transmute.distinction: Metamorphose suggests a natural change of form, as of a caterpillar, while transmute suggests changing one substance into another, as in alchemy.

meticulous|punctilious.distinction: Meticulous is careful about accuracy and detail, while punctilious is careful about correct form and procedure. One checks the figures, the other the protocol.

mitigate|palliate.distinction: Mitigate lessens the severity of the thing itself, while palliate only eases the symptoms and leaves the cause untouched.

mollify|placate.distinction: Mollify and placate both mean to calm someone's anger and are interchangeable, though placate more often implies a concession was made to do it.

monetary|pecuniary.distinction: Monetary is about money as a system, as in monetary policy, while pecuniary is about money as a personal interest or gain, as in a pecuniary motive.

morass|quagmire.distinction: A morass is a confusing mess you flounder in, while a quagmire is a situation that pulls you deeper the more you struggle. Quagmire suits a war.

morbid|pathological.distinction: Morbid is an unhealthy preoccupation with death and gloom, while pathological is a compulsion the person cannot control. A morbid interest, a pathological liar.

mordant|vitriolic.distinction: Mordant wit is biting and often admired for its sharpness, while vitriolic abuse is savage and meant to wound. One amuses, the other attacks.

morose|saturnine.distinction: Morose is gloomy and sullen in mood, while saturnine is a settled gloomy temperament, often with a sardonic edge. One is today, the other is always.

morose|sullen.distinction: Morose and sullen both mean gloomy and uncommunicative, though sullen carries more resentment and morose more settled unhappiness.

multifaceted|multifarious.distinction: Multifaceted means one thing with many sides, while multifarious means many things of different kinds. A multifaceted problem, a multifarious collection.

multitude|throng.distinction: A multitude is a great number of anything, while a throng is a crowd of people pressed together. Reasons come in a multitude, not a throng.

mundane|quotidian.distinction: Mundane stresses that a thing is dull and worldly, while quotidian stresses that it happens every day. Quotidian tasks need not be mundane.

munificent|unsparing.distinction: Munificent is always praise for lavish giving, while unsparing can mean either giving without limit or criticising without mercy.

munificent|unstinting.distinction: Munificent suggests giving on a grand scale, often of money, while unstinting suggests nothing at all was held back, often of effort or praise.

natty|raffish.distinction: Natty is neatly and smartly dressed, while raffish is stylish in a slightly disreputable way. Natty is respectable; raffish is not quite.

natty|rakish.distinction: Natty is about neat correct smartness, while rakish is about dash with a hint of scandal. A natty suit is pressed; a rakish hat is tilted.

negligent|remiss.distinction: Negligent is the word law uses for failing in a duty of care, while remiss is milder and usually describes a personal lapse one apologises for.

neophyte|tyro.distinction: Neophyte and tyro both mean beginner, though neophyte suggests someone newly initiated into a practice and tyro suggests raw inexperience at a skill.

nettlesome|peevish.distinction: Nettlesome describes a problem that irritates, while peevish describes a person who is irritable. A nettlesome question makes a peevish minister.

neutralize|nullify.distinction: Neutralize cancels an effect in practice, while nullify cancels something in law or in principle. An antidote neutralizes; a court nullifies.

nevertheless|notwithstanding.distinction: Nevertheless usually stands alone between clauses, while notwithstanding usually attaches to the obstacle itself, as in notwithstanding the delay.

nicety|nuance.distinction: A nicety is a fine point of procedure or manners, while a nuance is a shade of meaning or feeling. Legal niceties, a nuance of tone.

nostrum|panacea.distinction: A nostrum is a quack remedy someone is pushing, while a panacea is a supposed cure for everything. Nostrum always carries contempt; panacea may not.

nullify|quash.distinction: Nullify makes something void so it has no force, while quash is what a higher court does to a conviction or what authority does to a rebellion.

obdurate|obstinate.distinction: Obdurate suggests a heart hardened against appeal, while obstinate suggests a will that simply will not change course. Obdurate is the colder word.

obsolete|superannuated.distinction: Obsolete means superseded by something better, while superannuated means worn out by age. A format goes obsolete; a machine or a person is superannuated.

obstinate|wayward.distinction: Obstinate holds its ground and will not move, while wayward goes off in its own direction. One refuses to change course, the other refuses the course.

omnipresent|ubiquitous.distinction: Omnipresent carries a theological weight and suits God or dread, while ubiquitous is everyday and suits coffee shops and smartphones.

orotund|turgid.distinction: Orotund describes a voice that is rich, full and pompous, while turgid describes prose that is swollen and heavy to read. One is heard, the other is suffered.

ostensible|ostensive.distinction: Ostensible means the reason given rather than the real one, while ostensive means defining something by pointing at it. They share a root and almost nothing else.

pacify|placate.distinction: Pacify can mean to subdue a region by force as well as to calm a person, while placate only ever means to soothe someone's anger.

paean|panegyric.distinction: A paean is a joyful song of praise or thanksgiving, while a panegyric is a formal speech or essay in praise of someone. One is sung, the other delivered.

painstaking|scrupulous.distinction: Painstaking is about the effort taken over detail, while scrupulous adds moral exactness. A scrupulous accountant will not fudge; a painstaking one will not err.

palaver|rhetoric.distinction: Palaver is idle fuss and talk about nothing, while rhetoric is the art of persuasive language, contemptible only when it is empty.

pallid|wan.distinction: Pallid and wan both mean unhealthily pale, though wan adds weakness and exhaustion while pallid can also describe a feeble performance.

palpable|patent.distinction: Palpable means so strong you can almost touch it, while patent means so plain nobody could miss it. Palpable tension, a patent absurdity.

pedestrian|prosaic.distinction: Pedestrian suggests plodding without flair, while prosaic suggests the flatness of prose against poetry. Both mean dull, but pedestrian is the harsher verdict.

peevish|petulant.distinction: Peevish is habitual fretful complaining, while petulant is a childish sulk over a particular slight. One is a temperament, the other an outburst.

pellucid|perspicuous.distinction: Pellucid describes something transparent, whether water or prose, while perspicuous only describes expression that is easy to follow.

penchant|predilection.distinction: Penchant and predilection both name a settled liking, though predilection suggests a preference formed by taste and penchant a habitual inclination.

perilous|precarious.distinction: Perilous means dangerous, while precarious means unstable and liable to collapse. A precarious ledge is perilous because it may give way.

permeate|pervade.distinction: Permeate suits physical spreading through a substance, while pervade suits an atmosphere or influence spreading through a place or a work.

perpetual|unremitting.distinction: Perpetual means it never ends, while unremitting means it never slackens. Perpetual motion continues; unremitting pressure keeps its intensity.

perseverance|tenacity.distinction: Perseverance is keeping on through difficulty, while tenacity is refusing to let go of what one holds. One endures, the other grips.

persist|prevail.distinction: Persist is to keep going despite obstacles, while prevail is to win in the end or to be widespread. You can persist and never prevail.

perspicacious|sagacious.distinction: Perspicacious is sharpness at seeing what is there, while sagacious is wisdom in judging what to do. One notices, the other decides.

pertinacious|tenacious.distinction: Pertinacious carries a note of stubbornness that wearies others, while tenacious is usually admiring. A tenacious campaigner, a pertinacious complainer.

pinnacle|summit.distinction: Pinnacle is mostly figurative and names the height of achievement, while summit is literally a mountain top and also a meeting of heads of state.

placid|tranquil.distinction: Placid suits a temperament or a surface that nothing disturbs, while tranquil suits a scene or a mood that is peaceful. A placid cow, a tranquil evening.

plastic|pliant.distinction: Plastic means capable of being moulded into a new shape, while pliant means bending readily under pressure. One is reshaped, the other yields.

ploy|stratagem.distinction: A ploy is a single small tactic to gain an advantage, while a stratagem is a worked-out scheme, often involving deception of an opponent.

polemic|polemical.distinction: A polemic is the attacking piece itself, while polemical describes its tone. He wrote a polemic; the book is polemical.

pompous|pontifical.distinction: Pompous is self-importance in general, while pontifical is self-importance delivering opinions as though they were doctrine.

pompous|portentous.distinction: Pompous is inflated with self-importance, while portentous is heavy with supposed significance, and can also mean foreboding.
